Take-home · 7AI · Visual design

Designing for an agentic security investigation and using AI to develop trust.

The brief: a report page where a security analyst quickly sees how critical an alert is, what 7AI thinks of its severity, and what work 7AI did. Here is my method, what I used Claude for, and where I made the calls.

DeliverableOne screen

Plus a clickable prototype

ToolsFour tools

Figma, Claude, VS Code, Perplexity

AI's rolePartner

I set direction and checked its claims

Tools · where I used them
Perplexity

User research. I used it to find studies on SOC analysts: alert fatigue, how they check alerts, and whether they trust AI summaries.

Figma

Comments on the original, the 7AI design system as variables and components, the high-fidelity design, and the journey diagram.

Claude

Compared competitors, drew mid-fi wireframes, extracted the design system, ran the WCAG scan, redrew my journeys with suggestions, and vibe-coded the prototype.

VS Code

Text edits. I opened the HTML files for the prototype and this walkthrough and changed the words myself.

Method · click to jump
01 · Discovery & Brainstorming

Start with trust.

Three types of personas read this page. I worked out what each one needs to believe it.

What the research told me · found with Perplexity
~3,000

Analysts are flooded

Vendor surveys put daily alerts near 3,000 with most left unaddressed; a 2024 survey reports 62% ignored. Vendor-run, so I treat them as directional.

Vectra · Elastic

Context beats a label

SOC analysts check alarms against organizational context and evidence. A severity label alone isn’t enough.

Alahmadi et al., USENIX Security 2022

Explaining isn't verifying

Explanations alone didn't improve decisions, and AI summaries can omit or misstate key facts. So I designed for verification.

Roch et al., 2026 · Kramer et al., SOUPS 2025

Personas and jobs to be done
Tier 1 · Triage

Is it real, how bad, do I escalate?

Needs a verdict in about three seconds.

Tier 2 · Investigate

What happened, and how far did it spread?

Needs the evidence and the agent's trace.

SOC Leader · Oversight

Can I trust and audit this?

Needs a record of what was checked and decided.

Other brainstorming threads
Pull-request-style review, like GitHubLet an analyst override the verdictThe agent should investigate like a Tier 2 analystWhich integrations show up?

How AI helped. Claude found and summarized the studies and drafted the jobs to be done from the brief. I chose which evidence to lean on, flagged the vendor-run numbers, and kept a list of what the research does not prove.

    03 · Competitive Analysis

    Using patterns for inspiration.

    I looked at AI SOC analyst tools (Dropzone AI, Prophet Security, Exaforce, Qevlar, Intezer) and 7AI's own product with one question: how does each show the verdict, the evidence, and the work behind it?

    7AI's own product, as the benchmark
    What inspired me
    • Verdict and priority as separate signals
    • Evidence you can open and check
    • Plain-language step titles
    What I avoided
    • Red doing every job (priority, verdict, every highlight)
    • Dim, low-contrast text on dark
    • Dashboard density on a page meant for a quick read

    Screens are from Dropzone AI's public demo and 7ai.com, used for analysis only.

    How AI helped. I walked through the live demos and captured the screens. Claude helped me compare them against the three goals. I kept only the patterns that served the analyst.

    04 · Wireframing

    Sketch it, wireframe it, then build it.

    I started on paper, at low fidelity. Claude turned the sketch and the brief into a mid-fidelity wireframe I could rearrange. Then I built the high-fidelity design in Figma, on a 7AI design system I had to make first.

    Open the Figma file ↗
    The design system, as a markdown file

    There was no public 7AI design system, so I wrote one down.

    I didn't want to guess at 7AI's look, and I didn't want to invent my own. So I used Claude to pull the design properties and patterns out of the 7AI product platform: the product screens on 7ai.com, the screenshot in the brief, and the original Figma file.

    Claude sampled the colors, type, spacing, corner radii, and shadows, and listed the patterns the product repeats: status pills, the dashed agent rail, text links with a chevron, and 7AI's own words for a conclusion (Malicious, Suspicious, Mitigated). I captured all of it in one markdown file: tokens, components, and the rules for using them.

    That file became the source of truth. Claude read it and built it into Figma as variables: 38 color variables, spacing and radius, 13 text styles, and 2 shadow styles. Every component in the design is bound to them.

    It's a close reconstruction of 7AI's system, so the values are approximations.

    Optimizing for WCAG

    I had Claude check the design against WCAG AA, then fixed the tokens.

    WCAG has no single score. Each criterion passes or fails. So I asked Claude to scan every text layer in the Figma frame and check it against Level AA.

    The first scan: 109 of 172 text runs passed contrast (1.4.3), about 63%. Most of the failures came from a few tokens in the system I had just built: gray secondary text at about 4.1:1, and white on red pills at 3.25:1.

    • Secondary text went from #7b7b7b to #6b6b6b (5.3:1).
    • Red text went to #c62d2a (5.5:1), and the red pills got dark text (4.8:1).
    • The finding numbers and the note field's border were fixed too.

    Since everything was bound to variables, changing a few tokens fixed the whole design. The re-scan passed AA on every text run. Color never carries meaning alone (1.4.1), and buttons meet the 24px target size (2.5.8).

    I wanted more orange on the conclusion, and Claude pushed back: in 7AI's system, orange means Suspicious, and orange text fails contrast. I kept red. Figma can't test keyboard order, focus, or screen-reader names, so I built those into the prototype.

    From concepts to deliverables
    “View reasoning” on every signalAI sparkle on 7AI-written textOversight renamed AuditBreadcrumb matched to the product

    How AI helped. Claude drew both mid-fi wireframes from my paper sketch and the brief, one in Figma and one on its design canvas. It also pulled 7AI's design properties into my markdown file, built the Figma variables from it, and ran the WCAG scan. I moved things around, cut what repeated, decided what the page should say first, and chose which fixes to make.

    05 · Persona journeys

    I forgot the journeys. Going back made the design better.

    In the rush of the take-home, I went straight from personas to wireframes to Figma. I had three personas on my planning board, but I never mapped what each one actually does on this page. I flubbed that step, and it made me rethink my design.

    What the journeys showed me

    One page, three different jobs

    I had designed one page and assumed it served all three personas. Drawing the journeys made it obvious that it didn't. Each one shows up for a different reason, makes a different decision, and hands off to someone else.

    The handoffs were missing

    Tier 1's decision has to go somewhere. Tier 2 needs to know why a case reached them. The leader needs to see who decided what and why. My first design had buttons, but no path between people.

    My own open questions

    “Was it reviewed?” “Daily?” “Where did the analyst disagree with AI?” I wrote these on the sketch because I didn't have answers yet.

    What the generated journey suggested
    Answers to my questions
    • “Escalate to Tier 2?” Yes. Say where it goes and log it in the history.
    • “Was it reviewed?” Show who reviewed it, and when.
    • “Where did analysts disagree with AI?” Filter the audit trail by analyst and outcome.
    • “Daily?” A daily digest, or an alert only on exceptions.
    Gaps it found
    • Explain in plain words why Sentinel said Low and 7AI said Malicious.
    • Warn Tier 1 if they confirm without opening any evidence.
    • Containment isn't in the brief, so show what's recommended and what's been done.
    • Set a rule for when a case goes to the leader.
    What I didn't take
    • Sorting the alert queue by 7AI's conclusion
    • The leader's daily digest
    • Patterns across many investigations

    All good ideas, but they need data across many cases. They're bigger than one report page, so I kept them as stretch ideas.

    How it changed the design
    Tier 1 · Triage

    Decide, right in the summary.

    A short note explains why the ratings differ. The decision sits in the summary card: Confirm, or Escalate to a Tier 2 Analyst with a reason.

    Tier 2 · Investigate

    Start with why it's here.

    Under the signals, an amber note says who has the case right now. Amber matches the “Under review” pill. Red means Malicious, so I kept it out. Below that is the same “Why the ratings differ” note Tier 1 sees. The agent report is open, with Re-scan on each tool, and Remediation sits right below it.

    SOC Leader · Oversight

    A list first, then the case.

    The leader lands on a dashboard of the team's investigations and where they're needed, then opens a case. The case has no accordions. It looks like Tier 1 and Tier 2, with the decision chain, what was checked, and analyst disagreement added. One action, Review decision, records Approved or Disagreed with a note.

    The summary stays the same in all three views, so it still reads as one product. Only the order, the emphasis, and the main action change. I also tightened the words: “conclusion” for what 7AI finds, “decision” for what people do.

    From Figma to Claude to a clickable prototype
    1 · Figma

    Design it on the system

    I designed the page in Figma, with every layer bound to the 7AI variables.

    2 · Claude

    Read the file, write the code

    Claude read my Figma file and vibe-coded it into one working HTML file: real buttons, expandable sections, the entity map, and the audit trail.

    3 · Iterate

    Screenshot, note, change, check

    I clicked through it, marked up screenshots, and described each change in plain words. Claude made the change, and I checked it in the browser. For text edits, I opened the HTML in VS Code and changed the words myself.

    4 · Prototype

    Three views, one toggle

    The journey changes went in the same way. A small “View as” control sits outside the product, so you can switch personas without it looking like part of 7AI.

    How AI helped. Claude redrew my hand-drawn journeys as a Figma diagram and added the sticky-note suggestions, based on the brief and everything we'd discussed. Then it vibe-coded each change into the prototype. I drew the journeys, decided which suggestions to keep, and art-directed every round.
